Q: The important of some Escape Sequence Characters A:

In the example of horizontal tab, it's to help align columnar output in a text mode. The tab exists on old manual typewriters, too. Aligning to columns has been useful for financial ledgers for centuries.

The use of other escape sequences dates back to text-mode terminals used in the 1970's and 80's. Before graphical desktops, windows, and other user interface elements.

We used to develop simple user interfaces on text screens. Text could be placed anywhere on the screen, not just appending line by line. If you've used text editors like vim or emacs you've seen this. We even developed video games.

Terminals are by nature streaming bytes and writing them out on a screen in the order they were received. To write programs that place text anywhere on the screen, you need to be able to move the cursor backwards or up to previous lines.

A few cursor movements became standardized, like backspace. Others were not standard, and were implemented differently on different brands of text terminals. For the standard ones, languages like C added the escape sequences to make them easier to type, and subsequent languages usually adopted the same escape sequences.

Not as many people code screen graphics like that anymore, but programming languages still support those escape sequences because if they didn't, then millions of apps written for those terminals would no longer be supported.

Q: How to code a car shape of a F1 car moving on a track like F1 circuit A: 
The core issue is that your car doesn’t have a path to follow — it needs a waypoint system.

Basic concept:

1. Define waypoints around your circuit (array of x,y coordinates at each corner)
2. Car always moves toward the current waypoint
3. When car reaches a waypoint, target the next one
4. When all waypoints completed = 1 lap

For the car staying on path:
currentWaypoint = waypoints[index]
angle = atan2(target.y - car.y, 
              target.x - car.x)
car.x += cos(angle) * speed
car.y += sin(angle) * speed

if (distanceTo(currentWaypoint) < threshold):
    index = (index + 1) % waypoints.length
    if (index == 0): lapCount++

The more waypoints you define around the circuit shape, the smoother and more accurate the path will be.

Q: NextJS SSR in Capacitor A:

I am currently investigating the same. Looking to wrap an existing responsive web application based on nextjs using SSR.

in this blog I read in the comments that you can essentially point capacitor to any existing URL (so also your already running website).

I have not tested it though yet. My biggest questions right now would be:

  1. Could we still use native functions (such as push notifications, which is one of the main reasons of bundling it as an app) then? probably would need to integrate the required libs in my existing web app and check if we are running in capacitor environment somehow.
  2. How does Apple handle such cases upon submissions? I have read that they do reject apps that mainly just wrap existing web sites without offering any app-like advantages.
